title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Explain what deconvolution estimates, and what it cannot estimate
⚠️ Say why the reference dataset determines the answer, and what to check before trusting one
Distinguish a cell-type map from a niche map, and say why the second is where the biology usually is
⚠️ Test co-localisation against a null that respects tissue structure
⚠️ Say why neighbouring spots inflate significance, and what to do about it
Place any claim on the evidence ladder from description to demonstration
Design a spatial validation step for a hypothesis generated in W5–W6

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
1) The problem, restated
From 🔗 W7 §3: a Visium spot is a mixture. Deconvolution asks what mixture of cell types best explains the observed profile — using single-cell data as the dictionary of what each cell type looks like.



The reference is not a technical detail. It is the assumption the whole result rests on.










Method
Approach
Notes




RCTD
Statistical, models platform effects
robust, widely used


cell2location
Bayesian, estimates absolute abundance
✅ gives cell numbers, not only proportions


CARD
Uses spatial correlation between spots
borrows information from neighbours


SPOTlight
NMF-based
fast


Tangram
Maps single cells onto space
useful when you have matched data



💡 Method choice matters less than reference choice. Benchmarks separate these methods by modest margins; a wrong reference changes the answer entirely.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Reference bias






ImportantThe failure mode with no error message





Deconvolution returns proportions that sum to one over the cell types you supplied. It has no way to report “there is something here I have never seen”.

⚠️ A cell type absent from the reference does not appear as missing. Its signal is redistributed onto whichever reference type is closest. This is the single-cell version of reference bias, one layer down
⚠️ A reference from healthy tissue applied to tumour, or from PBMCs applied to tissue-resident cells, biases every proportion at once — not just the affected type
⚠️ A reference from a different platform (Smart-seq vs 10x, cells vs nuclei) carries systematic differences into the estimates

✅ What to actually check:

Same tissue, same condition, ideally the same patients as the spatial sections
Verify with a marker gene you did not deconvolve — plot raw CD3E and see whether it lands where the T-cell proportions did
Ask whether a rare-but-important population is in the reference at all

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
section: 3) What proportions can and cannot tell you
text:
3) What proportions can and cannot tell you

✅ “This region is enriched for macrophage signal relative to that region” — solid
✅ “Macrophage proportion correlates with distance from the invasion front” — solid, and interesting
⚠️ “This spot contains 2.3 macrophages” — only cell2location-style methods attempt absolute numbers, and with wide uncertainty
❌ “These particular macrophages express gene X” — you cannot get cell-type-specific expression out of a mixture without much stronger assumptions

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
section: 1) The question that spatial data is actually for
text:
1) The question that spatial data is actually for
A per-spot cell-type map is useful, and it is still one location at a time. The step that uses the geometry is asking what each location is surrounded by.



The interface exists only as a mixture. No single spot defines it.


How it works: for each spot, build a vector of the cell-type composition of its neighbours (within k spots or a fixed radius), then cluster those vectors. The clusters are niches — recurrent tissue microenvironments.
💡 Notice what the left panel hides. T cells and macrophages are present almost everywhere and dominate almost nowhere, so a “dominant cell type” map erases them entirely. The immune biology is invisible until you look at composition rather than identity.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Testing co-localisation honestly






WarningAgainst which null?





“Cell type A and cell type B co-occur more than expected” requires a definition of expected.

❌ Complete spatial randomness is the wrong null. Tissue is not random — it has layers, vessels, capsules, glands. Almost any two cell types will beat this null
✅ Permute labels within the tissue, preserving the overall architecture and each cell type’s total abundance
✅ Or compare against matched control tissue — the same anatomy, different disease state

⚠️ And back to the motivating question: p < 10⁻¹² across 4,000 spots is mostly telling you that you had 4,000 spots. Neighbouring spots are positively correlated by construction (🔗 W7 §4.3), so the effective sample size is far smaller than the nominal one.
→ ✅ The number that matters is the effect size, replicated across patients.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
3) Mapping single cells into space
The reverse direction: take a cluster you found in scRNA-seq and ask where it sits.

Tangram, Seurat anchor transfer — project single-cell labels onto spatial data
✅ Genuinely useful for testing a specific hypothesis: “the exhausted CD8 state we found — is it inside the tumour or at the margin?”
⚠️ Circularity risk: if the mapping uses the same genes that defined the cluster, finding the cluster is not independent evidence

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
1) Deconvolve, then check the reference

library(Seurat); library(spacexr); library(tidyverse)   # spacexr = RCTD

sp  <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "7_visium.rds"))
ref <- readRDS(here::here("analysis", "5_pbmc_annotated.rds"))   # ⚠️ is this the right reference?

reference <- Reference(GetAssayData(ref, "counts"), factor(ref$cell_type))
puck      <- SpatialRNA(GetTissueCoordinates(sp), GetAssayData(sp, "counts"))

rctd <- create.RCTD(puck, reference, max_cores = 4) |> run.RCTD(doublet_mode = "full")
props <- normalize_weights(rctd@results$weights)

⚠️ Before believing any of it, ask what a PBMC reference implies for a tissue section. Tissue-resident macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelium are not in it — where did their signal go?

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
section: 2) ✅ The verification that should be reflexive
text:
2) ✅ The verification that should be reflexive

# Plot a raw marker gene next to the estimated proportion of its cell type
p1 <- SpatialFeaturePlot(sp, features = "CD3E") + ggtitle("raw CD3E")
sp$Tcell_prop <- props[, "CD8 T"]
p2 <- SpatialFeaturePlot(sp, features = "Tcell_prop") + ggtitle("estimated CD8 T")
p1 | p2

💡 If these two maps disagree, the deconvolution is telling you about your reference, not about the tissue.

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
3) Niches

library(FNN)

coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(sp)
nn     <- get.knn(as.matrix(coords), k = 6)$nn.index

# neighbourhood composition per spot
nbr_comp <- t(apply(nn, 1, \(idx) colMeans(props[idx, , drop = FALSE])))

set.seed(1)
sp$niche <- factor(kmeans(nbr_comp, centers = 5)$cluster)
SpatialDimPlot(sp, group.by = "niche")

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
4) ✅ Change one thing

# Does your co-localisation survive a structure-preserving null?
observed <- cor(props[, "CD8 T"], props[, "Macrophage"])

null <- replicate(1000, {
  perm <- sample(nrow(props))          # ⚠️ a naive permutation — discuss why this is still too easy
  cor(props[perm, "CD8 T"], props[, "Macrophage"])
})

cat("observed:", round(observed, 3),
    " null 95%:", round(quantile(null, c(.025, .975)), 3), "\n")

⚠️ Then discuss: this permutation destroys all tissue structure, so it is the too-easy null from §2.2. What would a better one look like? (Hint: permute within anatomical region, or shift the whole label map rigidly.)

title: W8. Deconvolution & Spatial Integration
text:
5) Before next week
W9 — proteomics. Everything so far measured RNA. Next we ask whether the protein was ever made — and find out how often the answer is no.
Nothing to install; W9 is conceptual.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Say why mRNA is a limited proxy for protein, and quantify how limited
Describe what a mass spectrometer measures, in one paragraph, without hand-waving
⚠️ Explain why DDA produces missing values that look like biology
Say why plasma is the hardest and most clinically useful sample in proteomics
Choose between mass spectrometry and an affinity panel for a given question
⚠️ Recognise the epitope artifact that produces false pQTLs
Ask a proteomics core the three questions that determine whether your study will work

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 1) How well does mRNA predict protein?
text:
1) How well does mRNA predict protein?



Eight weeks of transcriptomics, and this is the strength of the link to the molecules that do the work.


Across genes within a sample, mRNA and protein abundance typically correlate at roughly r = 0.4–0.6. Correlation across samples for a single gene varies enormously — strong for some genes, effectively zero for others.






ImportantNeither result in the motivating question is wrong





They are measurements of different things.

RNA-seq measured transcription plus transcript stability
The protein assay measured the balance of translation, folding, secretion and degradation

A 3-fold mRNA increase with no protein change is a real, interpretable finding: something downstream is buffering it. That is often more interesting than agreement would have been.
⚠️ The mistake is not the discrepancy. The mistake is having written the RNA-seq result as if it were a statement about protein.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) Why this matters clinically, not just technically
text:
2) Why this matters clinically, not just technically

Drugs act on proteins. A target nominated purely from transcript data has skipped a step
Every biomarker you order — troponin, PSA, CRP, HbA1c — is a protein or a protein modification
Post-translational modification is invisible to RNA-seq. Phosphorylation, cleavage and glycosylation change what a protein does without changing how much of it there is
Secretion is invisible too. A cell can transcribe a cytokine and never release it (🔗 W6 §3)

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
1) The measurement, honestly
A mass spectrometer does not read protein sequences. It weighs charged fragments extremely precisely, and software infers sequences from the weights.
protein mixture
   → digest with trypsin        (proteins are too big; peptides are not)
   → liquid chromatography      (separate peptides in time)
   → MS1: weigh the peptides    (a survey of what is eluting now)
   → MS2: fragment and weigh    (the fragment pattern identifies the sequence)
   → match against a database   → protein identities and amounts
⚠️ Three consequences of this design that matter downstream:

You measure peptides and infer proteins. Peptides shared between family members create ambiguity
Identification depends on a database. A protein form not in the database is not found
Quantification is relative unless you spike in labelled standards

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) ⚠️ DDA and DIA — the distinction that decides your statistics
text:
2) ⚠️ DDA and DIA — the distinction that decides your statistics



The same instrument, two acquisition strategies, very different data.








WarningWhy DDA missingness is dangerous





In DDA the instrument selects the most intense precursors in each cycle. What is “most intense” depends on everything else co-eluting at that instant.

⚠️ The same sample run twice yields partly different protein lists
⚠️ Across a cohort, whether a protein was sampled correlates with total protein load, chromatography drift, and run order
⚠️ If cases and controls were run in different batches (🔗 W1 §3.3), missingness itself becomes a group difference

→ ✅ DIA fragments everything in fixed windows, so the same proteins are quantified in every run. For any clinical cohort, this is the right default — and it is the first thing to ask about someone else’s dataset.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
1) ⚠️ Affinity assays measure binding






ImportantThe epitope artifact, and why it matters in W11





An antibody or aptamer reports how much reagent bound. Usually that tracks protein abundance. Sometimes it does not.
A coding variant that alters the binding epitope reduces the signal without changing the amount of protein present. In a genetic analysis this appears as a variant that “lowers protein levels” — a false pQTL, and one that is strongly enriched for cis variants because those are the ones inside the gene.
✅ The check: for any cis-pQTL, ask whether the lead variant is a protein-altering variant in that same gene. If it is, the finding needs orthogonal confirmation — ideally by MS, which measures peptides directly.
⚠️ This matters because pQTLs are increasingly used for drug-target Mendelian randomization (🔗 W3 §3.2). An artifact here propagates into a target nomination.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
2) Cross-platform disagreement is normal
Studies comparing affinity platforms with each other, and with MS, routinely find that a substantial fraction of targets correlate poorly.

⚠️ Two papers reporting different results for the same protein may both be right about what they measured
✅ When it matters, confirm on a second platform. That is a reviewer-proof sentence in a methods section

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 1) Look up a protein you order
text:
1) Look up a protein you order
Human Protein Atlas → search a biomarker you use clinically (troponin I, PSA, CA-125, NT-proBNP…).

① Which tissues and cell types express it? Is it as specific as the clinical framing implies?
② Compare the RNA and protein tissue profiles on the same page. Where do they disagree?
③ Look at the pathology section — is expression associated with survival in any cancer?

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
section: 2) Check a proteomics dataset before trusting it
text:
2) Check a proteomics dataset before trusting it
Pick any plasma proteomics paper in your field and answer:

④ Platform? MS or affinity — and if MS, DDA or DIA?
⑤ Depletion? How many proteins were quantified, and does that number make sense for the sample type?
⑥ Missing values — how many, and how were they handled? (This is W10 §1)
⑦ Pre-analytical — were cases and controls collected the same way, in the same place?
⑧ Batches — were groups randomised across them, or stated at all?

💡 ⑦ and ⑧ are usually either in the supplement or absent. Absence is itself an answer.

title: W9. Proteomics — How Proteins Are Actually Measured
text:
3) Design task
Write five sentences specifying a proteomics study you could realistically run in your department: sample type, platform, n, comparison, and the one pre-analytical variable you are most worried about.
We will use these in W10.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Explain why missing values in proteomics are not missing at random, and how the choice of imputation changes conclusions
Run a differential abundance analysis with limma and say why it is not just a t-test
⚠️ Place a biomarker claim on the discovery → verification → validation → clinical ladder
⚠️ Recognise the wrong-control-group error, and design around it
Say what an AUC of 0.94 in a discovery study is worth
Distinguish diagnostic, prognostic and predictive biomarkers — and say which one a study actually tested
Write the design for a biomarker study you could run in your own department

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
1) Why they are not random
A protein is missing from a run mostly because it was below the limit of detection — that is, because it was low. Statisticians call this MNAR (missing not at random), and it is the opposite of the assumption most default methods make.

⚠️ DDA adds a second, technical layer of missingness on top (🔗 W9 §2.2) — a protein can be absent because it was not selected, not because it was low
✅ DIA data is much cleaner in this respect, which is most of why it is now the default

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 2) The four choices, and what each does to your result
text:
2) The four choices, and what each does to your result






ImportantEach one is an assumption, not a cleaning step






❌ Drop any protein with a missing value. You keep only the abundant, ubiquitously detected proteins — which is exactly the opposite of the set a novel biomarker would come from
❌ Impute with the row mean. Low values get pulled up toward the middle, shrinking precisely the difference you are testing
⚠️ Impute from a low distribution (e.g. a shifted, narrowed normal, as in Perseus). Usually a reasonable match to the MNAR mechanism — and still an assumption that belongs in the methods section
✅ Model missingness explicitly — MSstats, or report a presence/absence test alongside the intensity test. Most defensible, because it stops pretending the NAs are not data

💡 The reflexive check: rerun with a different imputation and see whether your hit survives. If it does not, you have learned something important before a reviewer does.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 1) Why limma and not a t-test
text:
1) Why limma and not a t-test
Proteomics datasets are wide and short — thousands of proteins, tens of samples. A per-protein t-test is unstable because each variance estimate rests on very few observations.
limma uses empirical Bayes to shrink each protein’s variance toward the overall trend. In practice this means a protein that happens to look very consistent by chance is not automatically declared significant.

library(limma); library(tidyverse)

# mat: log2 intensities, proteins × samples. meta: one row per sample.
design <- model.matrix(~ condition + sex + age + batch, data = meta)   # ⚠️ batch belongs here

fit <- lmFit(mat, design) |> eBayes(trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)
res <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditionCase", number = Inf) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "protein")


✅ trend = TRUE accounts for the intensity–variance relationship typical of MS data
⚠️ Include batch, sex and age in the design. Leaving them out does not make them go away
✅ For MS designs with technical replicates or fractionation, MSstats models the hierarchy properly

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
2) What to report

Effect size (log2 fold change) and adjusted p-value — the same discipline as DESeq2 last semester
How many proteins were tested, and how many were dropped for missingness. ⚠️ Multiple testing is over the proteins you tested, not the ones that survived (🔗 W2 §2.4)
Whether the result survives a different imputation

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 1) Three kinds of biomarker, often confused
text:
1) Three kinds of biomarker, often confused








Type
Asks
Requires




Diagnostic
Does this patient have the disease now?
Cases and the right differential diagnosis, at presentation


Prognostic
What will happen to this patient?
Follow-up, outcomes, and a survival model


Predictive
Will this patient respond to this drug?
⚠️ A treated and an untreated arm — otherwise you cannot separate prediction from prognosis



⚠️ Predictive is the hardest and the most often claimed. “Responders had higher levels than non-responders” is compatible with the marker simply indicating better-prognosis disease, regardless of treatment.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 2) ⚠️ Why an AUC of 0.94 can be worthless
text:
2) ⚠️ Why an AUC of 0.94 can be worthless



The number is real. The study answered a question nobody asks.








WarningBack to the motivating question





No — not from that study.
The paper compared advanced cancer with healthy volunteers. Your patient is neither. To be useful in your clinic, the marker must separate early cancer from the conditions that mimic it, sampled at presentation.
And there is a second problem hiding underneath. If cases were bled in an oncology ward and controls at a screening centre, then collection tube, time to processing and fasting state all differ systematically between groups (🔗 W9 §5). Some of that AUC is measuring where the blood was drawn.
→ ✅ Ask: were cases and controls sampled at the same point in the care pathway, in the same place, into the same tubes?

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 3) Prevalence changes everything at the bedside
text:
3) Prevalence changes everything at the bedside
AUC is prevalence-independent; positive predictive value is not.
Sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%:

  prevalence 50% (a trial cohort)   →  PPV ≈ 90%
  prevalence  1% (a screening clinic) →  PPV ≈  8%
⚠️ The same test. Ninety-two false positives per hundred positive results, and every one of them gets a CT scan.
💡 This is the calculation you can do and the bioinformatician cannot — because it needs the prevalence in your clinic.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
1) Handle the missingness deliberately

library(tidyverse); library(limma)

prot <- readRDS(here::here("rawdata", "plasma_proteomics.rds"))  # proteins × samples, log2
meta <- readRDS(here::here("rawdata", "plasma_meta.rds"))

# ⚠️ Look before deciding
miss <- rowMeans(is.na(prot))
hist(miss, breaks = 40, main = "Fraction missing per protein")

# Is missingness related to abundance? (if yes → MNAR)
plot(rowMeans(prot, na.rm = TRUE), miss,
     xlab = "mean intensity", ylab = "fraction missing", pch = 16, col = "#185FA5")

💡 A clear negative trend in that second plot is the MNAR evidence. Show it in your supplement.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
section: 2) Test, with the covariates that matter
text:
2) Test, with the covariates that matter

keep <- miss < 0.30                       # state this threshold in the methods
mat  <- prot[keep, ]

design <- model.matrix(~ condition + age + sex + batch, data = meta)
fit    <- lmFit(mat, design) |> eBayes(trend = TRUE, robust = TRUE)
res    <- topTable(fit, coef = "conditionCase", number = Inf) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "protein")

sum(res$adj.P.Val < 0.05)

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
3) ✅ Change one thing — three times

# ① Drop batch from the design. How many hits change?
# ② Impute from a low distribution instead of filtering. Do the top 10 survive?
# ③ Split by patient into train/test, fit on train, evaluate AUC on test.
#    Compare that AUC with the one from the full dataset.

⚠️ ③ is the important one. The gap between the in-sample AUC and the held-out AUC is the size of your overfitting, and it is usually larger than people expect.

title: W10. Clinical Proteomics & Biomarkers
text:
4) Design task, continued
Take the five sentences you wrote in 🔗 W9 §6.3 and add:

the comparator group you would actually need
the decision the result would change
the prevalence of the condition in the clinic where it would be used

Bring it to W14 — this is a legitimate capstone project.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Distinguish sequential from joint integration, and say which your question needs
Use convergent evidence across layers to narrow a locus to a single candidate gene
⚠️ Say why an absent signal in one layer is not a negative result
Read a MOFA variance-explained plot, and ⚠️ recognise a technical factor
⚠️ Anticipate the three failures that happen before any model is fitted: n collapse, scale imbalance, uninterpretable factors
Say what integration genuinely buys, and what it cannot manufacture

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
section: 1) Sequential — each layer filters the last
text:
1) Sequential — each layer filters the last
You already did this without calling it integration. W3 narrowed a locus; W5 named a cell type; W9 asked whether the protein exists. Each layer removes candidates.

✅ Keeps your full n at every step, because each analysis uses only the samples that have that layer
✅ Every step is interpretable on its own and defensible in a methods section
✅ Layers can come from different cohorts — public eQTL data, a published atlas, your own samples
⚠️ Cannot discover a pattern that only exists across layers

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
2) Joint — model the layers together
MOFA+, mixOmics/DIABLO, iCluster and similar methods find latent factors that explain variance across several layers at once.

✅ Can reveal coordinated programmes no single layer shows
✅ Unsupervised — can find structure you did not ask about (patient subtypes)
⚠️ Needs the same samples measured on every layer
⚠️ Output is a factor, not a mechanism

💡 Answer to the motivating question: usually no, not first. Sequential prioritisation answers most clinical questions, keeps your n, and produces a figure a reviewer can follow. Reach for joint modelling when you specifically suspect a cross-layer programme, or when you want unsupervised patient subtypes.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) Why convergence is strong evidence
Each layer has its own false positives, and they are largely independent: an eQTL colocalisation artifact has nothing to do with a proteomics artifact. A gene surviving five independent filters is unlikely to be five separate coincidences.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
section: 2) ⚠️ Why an absence is not evidence
text:
2) ⚠️ Why an absence is not evidence






ImportantThe asymmetry that gets misread constantly





A ✕ in one column almost always means “not measured in the right context”, not “measured and absent”.

⚠️ eQTL panels come from bulk tissue — effects confined to a rare cell type are invisible
⚠️ Plasma proteomics misses low-abundance proteins entirely (🔗 W9 §3)
⚠️ Some genes have no protein product to measure
⚠️ MR needs a strong instrument; a gene without one cannot be tested, which is not the same as being tested and failing

→ ✅ Report convergence as positive evidence. Report gaps as coverage limitations, in a sentence, in the results.
⚠️ And the failure mode this creates: prioritisation pipelines systematically favour well-measured, well-studied genes. The same bias returns in W12 as network hubs.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) What a factor is
A latent axis along which samples vary, together with loadings saying which features in which layers drive it. The variance-explained plot says how much of each layer each factor accounts for.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
2) ⚠️ Annotate factors before interpreting them






WarningFactor 1 is almost always technical





The strongest shared source of variation in a real cohort is rarely disease. It is batch, RNA integrity, sex, or age.
✅ The annotation routine, in order:

Technical — batch, run date, RIN/DV200, operator, storage time
Demographic — age, sex, BMI, ancestry
Clinical confounders — medication, comorbidity, disease duration
Only then — disease status or outcome

⚠️ If a factor correlates with batch at r = 0.8 and with disease at r = 0.3, it is a batch factor that happens to be slightly confounded with disease. Reporting it as a “disease signature” is a real and common error.
💡 A factor that loads across several layers is more likely to be biological than one confined to a single layer — but only after steps 1–3 come back empty.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
1) Build a prioritisation table
Take one locus for a disease you treat, and fill in the table from §2 by hand, in the browser:

eQTL — Open Targets Genetics or GTEx
Cell type — CELLxGENE
Protein — Human Protein Atlas
Direction — IEU OpenGWAS for MR results
Tractability — Open Targets target profile

✅ One row per candidate gene, one column per layer. This is an afternoon, and it is a real figure.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
2) Check the intersection first

library(tidyverse); library(UpSetR)

have <- meta |> transmute(
  clinical   = 1L,
  genotype   = as.integer(!is.na(geno_id)),
  rna        = as.integer(!is.na(rna_id)),
  proteomics = as.integer(!is.na(prot_id)))

upset(as.data.frame(have), order.by = "freq")
cat("complete cases:", sum(rowSums(have) == ncol(have)), "\n")   # ⚠️ this is your n

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
3) MOFA, and annotating its factors

library(MOFA2)

mofa <- create_mofa(list(RNA = rna_mat, Protein = prot_mat, Methyl = meth_mat)) |>
  prepare_mofa() |> run_mofa()

plot_variance_explained(mofa)          # the figure above

# ⚠️ the step that must come next
Z <- get_factors(mofa)[[1]]
covars <- meta |> select(batch, RIN, age, sex, bmi, condition)

cors <- sapply(covars, \(v) apply(Z, 2, \(f) {
  if (is.numeric(v)) abs(cor(f, v, use = "pairwise")) else summary(aov(f ~ factor(v)))[[1]][1, "F value"]
}))
round(cors, 2)     # look here before you look at biology

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
4) ✅ Change one thing

# Re-run MOFA with the batch effect removed from each layer first.
# Does Factor 1 disappear? Does anything else change rank?

💡 If removing batch reshuffles your factors, that tells you how much of the original result was batch — a number worth knowing before it appears in review.

title: W11. Multi-omics Integration
text:
5) Before next week
W12 — networks and drug targets. Bring the prioritisation table from §5.1. We will ask whether the surviving gene is druggable.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Say what a biological network is built from, and ⚠️ why that construction biases every result
⚠️ Recognise the study-bias artifact behind most “hub gene” findings
Compare the three routes to drug repurposing, and say what each is worth as evidence
⚠️ Explain why direction of effect decides agonist versus antagonist
Work through six questions that separate a top-ranked gene from an actual target
Use PheWAS and loss-of-function carriers as a free safety readout

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) The construction, and the bias it creates
text:
1) The construction, and the bias it creates
A protein–protein interaction network is an accumulation of published experiments. STRING, BioGRID and IntAct are curated literature, plus predictions trained on that literature.
Experiments concentrate on genes people already study. So node degree tracks publication count.



The correlation is not subtle.








ImportantThe answer to the motivating question is: not at all surprised





TP53, EGFR and AKT1 come out as hubs for nearly every disease that has ever been networked. They have tens of thousands of papers each, so they have edges to everything.
⚠️ Concretely, this means:

“Hub” analyses rediscover the same genes regardless of your data
Network proximity scores favour well-studied drugs and well-studied targets
Genes with no publications have degree ≈ 0 and can never be prioritised, however important

✅ What to do:

Compare against a degree-matched null — permute while preserving each node’s degree, so “well-connected” stops being an automatic win
Prefer networks built from a single systematic experiment (a proteomics interactome, a CRISPR screen) over literature aggregates, where you can
✅ Report degree alongside any hub claim, and let the reader see it

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 2) What networks are still good for
text:
2) What networks are still good for

✅ Modules — a set of genes that interact more than expected, giving a process-level rather than gene-level result
✅ Connecting your hits — do your 40 GWAS loci converge on a pathway?
✅ Suggesting a mechanism for a gene of unknown function, from its neighbours
⚠️ Always as a hypothesis. The edges are other people’s experiments, not yours

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) Genetic support is the strongest route
text:
1) Genetic support is the strongest route
Targets with human genetic support are roughly twice as likely to succeed through clinical development. The mechanism is simple: a variant that alters the target is a natural, lifelong, randomised experiment in humans — the argument from 🔗 W3 §3.2.

PCSK9 — loss-of-function carriers have low LDL and low cardiovascular risk → inhibitors work
IL6R — a variant mimicking IL-6 blockade associates with lower CHD risk → tocilizumab’s cardiovascular signal

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
2) ⚠️ Direction of effect






WarningThe mistake with the worst consequences in this course





If the risk allele increases target activity, you want an inhibitor. If it decreases it, the target may be protective — and inhibiting it would make patients worse.
Two complications:

⚠️ Incoherence. A risk allele can down-regulate a gene that appears up-regulated in patients. Often that is an impaired protective response, and the therapeutic direction is the opposite of what the expression data suggests
⚠️ Tissue-specificity. Direction can differ between tissues. The relevant tissue is the one where the disease process happens (🔗 W5, 🔗 W7)

→ ✅ Establish direction from genetics plus MR, not from a fold change in patient tissue.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
3) Signature reversal and network proximity

Signature reversal (CMap, LINCS) — find a drug whose expression signature is anti-correlated with the disease signature. ⚠️ Reference profiles come from cell lines at high doses. Useful for generating candidates; not evidence
Network proximity — is a drug’s target close to the disease module? ⚠️ Inherits every bias in §1, so it needs a degree-matched null to mean anything

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 1) No code: profile your surviving gene
text:
1) No code: profile your surviving gene
Open Targets → your gene → its target profile.

① Tractability — small molecule? antibody? Which clinical phase, for any indication?
② Safety — any flagged organ toxicity?
③ Known drugs — is something already approved against it, for anything?
④ gnomAD → LOEUF. Is the gene tolerant of loss of function?
⑤ Open Targets Genetics → PheWAS for the lead variant. What else does it affect?

✅ Write the answers as five sentences. That is §3’s checklist, done.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
section: 2) Build a small network, then check yourself
text:
2) Build a small network, then check yourself

library(STRINGdb); library(igraph); library(tidyverse)

sdb <- STRINGdb$new(version = "12", species = 9606, score_threshold = 700)
mapped <- sdb$map(data.frame(gene = my_genes), "gene", removeUnmappedRows = TRUE)
g <- sdb$get_subnetwork(mapped$STRING_id) |> igraph::simplify()

deg <- sort(degree(g), decreasing = TRUE)
head(deg, 10)

⚠️ Now the step that is usually missing:

# Is your "hub" just a well-studied gene?
# Fetch PubMed counts for the same genes and correlate with degree.
pubs <- readRDS(here::here("rawdata", "pubmed_counts.rds"))   # gene → n papers
cor(log10(pubs[names(deg)] + 1), deg, use = "complete", method = "spearman")

💡 In most literature-derived networks this correlation is strong. Report it, and your hub claim becomes credible instead of automatic.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
3) A degree-matched null

observed <- mean(distances(g, v = disease_genes, to = drug_targets))

null <- replicate(1000, {
  rw <- sample_degseq(degree(g), method = "vl")   # same degrees, rewired edges
  mean(distances(rw, v = disease_genes, to = drug_targets))
})

cat("observed:", round(observed, 2), " null mean:", round(mean(null), 2), "\n")

✅ If the observed proximity is not clearly better than the degree-matched null, you have measured popularity.

title: W12. Network Analysis & Drug Targets
text:
4) Before next week
W13 — interpretation and visualisation. Bring one figure from your own work or from a paper you are reading. We will take it apart.

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

⚠️ Spot the four ways a figure routinely overstates its data
Choose a chart form from the job the data has to do
⚠️ Say why “enriched for immune response” is almost never a result
Set the right background for an enrichment test, and say why it changes the answer
Write a figure caption as one sentence — before drawing the figure
Decide what belongs in a main figure and what belongs in the supplement

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
1) The others, briefly

⚠️ Truncated axes. For bars, always start at zero — a bar’s length is the value. If zero is uninformative, use points or a dot plot instead
⚠️ Rainbow colour maps. Not perceptually ordered, invent boundaries where data is smooth, and fail in greyscale and for colour-vision deficiency. ✅ Use a single-hue sequential ramp for magnitude, and a two-hue diverging ramp with a neutral midpoint for signed values
⚠️ Bars that hide n. With n ≤ 10, ✅ plot the individual points. A bar plus SEM at n = 3 implies a precision you do not have

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
section: 1) The background is the whole test
text:
1) The background is the whole test
Enrichment asks whether your gene list contains more of a category than expected by chance from some universe. Change the universe, change the answer.

❌ Default “all human genes” — but genes not expressed in your tissue could never have been in your list
✅ The universe is the genes you actually tested: expressed above threshold, passing filters
⚠️ In tissue-specific data this typically halves the universe, and it can remove an entire “significant” category


library(clusterProfiler); library(org.Hs.eg.db)

universe <- rownames(dds)[rowSums(counts(dds)) > 10]   # ✅ what was testable

ego <- enrichGO(gene = sig_genes, universe = universe,     # ⚠️ not the default
                OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL",
                ont = "BP", pAdjustMethod = "BH")

ego <- simplify(ego, cutoff = 0.7)     # collapse redundant nested terms

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
2) GSEA on the ranked list
✅ Often better than an over-representation test: it uses the whole ranking rather than a thresholded list, so there is no arbitrary cut-off, and modest coordinated shifts are detectable.

ranks <- res |> filter(!is.na(stat)) |> arrange(desc(stat)) |>
  select(gene, stat) |> deframe()

gseaGO <- gseGO(ranks, OrgDb = org.Hs.eg.db, keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP")

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
3) ⚠️ Then name genes
“Enriched for immune response” is compatible with almost any inflammatory tissue. “Interferon signalling, driven by IFI44L, ISG15 and MX1” is a sentence a reader can act on — and check.

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
section: 1) Take apart the figure you brought
text:
1) Take apart the figure you brought
Work in pairs. For your neighbour’s figure:

① Write the caption as one sentence. Can you?
② Does the axis start at zero, and should it?
③ Can you see the n? Can you see individual patients?
④ If there is a heatmap: how were the genes chosen, and was it row-scaled?
⑤ If there is a colour scale: sequential, diverging, or rainbow — and does it match the job?
⑥ Which panel could move to the supplement without weakening the point?

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
text:
2) Rebuild one plot

library(tidyverse)

# ❌ before
ggplot(d, aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col") +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = .2)

# ✅ after — the patients are visible, and n is on the axis
d |>
  mutate(group = fct_relevel(group, "control")) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .45, outlier.shape = NA, colour = "#8A7FA3") +
  geom_jitter(width = .12, size = 2.6, alpha = .85, colour = "#185FA5") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "\n(n = ", table(d$group)[x], ")")) +
  labs(y = "CD8 T-cell fraction", x = NULL,
       title = "Responders have a higher CD8 T-cell fraction") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

title: W13. Interpretation & Visualisation
section: 3) Redo an enrichment with the right universe
text:
3) Redo an enrichment with the right universe

# Run enrichGO twice: default universe, then the expressed-gene universe.
# How many terms survive? Does the top term change?

💡 This takes two minutes and changes results often enough to be worth doing every time.

text:
4) Before next week
W14 — your own project. Bring a one-sentence research question and a note of what data you could realistically get hold of.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
Note🎯 Learning objectives





By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

Narrow a broad interest into a question with a comparison, a measurement and a data source
⚠️ Judge feasibility honestly, and recognise the quadrant where most first projects die
Plan four figures before running any analysis
State which rung of the evidence ladder your project can reach, and name the next one
⚠️ Say why a negative result is a complete project
Leave with a written one-page protocol

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
section: 1) What “data you already have” actually includes
text:
1) What “data you already have” actually includes
Residents consistently underestimate this list:

✅ The pathology archive — FFPE blocks with linked outcomes. Spatial and proteomics both work on FFPE (🔗 W7 §2.2)
✅ Residual clinical samples — banked serum or plasma, under existing consent in some institutions
✅ The EHR — labs, imaging reports, medications, outcomes, already digital
✅ Public data collected for another purpose — GEO, CELLxGENE, TCGA, the UK Biobank return files. A dataset generated to answer question A very often contains the answer to your question B
✅ Your department’s own past studies — data that was analysed once, for one aim

💡 The best resident projects usually combine one existing dataset with one clinical question nobody in the original study cared about.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
2) The honest costs







Step
Realistic time




IRB / ethics for archived samples
⚠️ 1–4 months, and it starts the clock


Locating and pulling blocks
2–6 weeks, and someone must do it


Sectioning, QC (DV200)
2–4 weeks


Assay turnaround at a core
4–12 weeks


Analysis
⚠️ Always longer than planned


Writing
Longer still



⚠️ Start the ethics application in week one. It is the only step that cannot be compressed by working harder.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
1) Name your rung
From 🔗 W8 §3: description → hypothesis → consistent with → supported → demonstrated.
A resident project realistically reaches ③ consistent with. That is publishable, fundable, and honest — provided you say so and name the experiment that would take it to ④ or ⑤.
⚠️ What sinks projects at review is not stopping at ③. It is writing ⑤’s verb over ③’s evidence.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
section: 2) ✅ A negative result is a complete project
text:
2) ✅ A negative result is a complete project






TipWhat makes a negative result complete





Not “we found nothing”. Rather:

✅ The hypothesis was specific enough to be wrong
✅ The design could have detected the effect — say how large an effect you had power for
✅ The measurement worked — positive controls behaved as expected
✅ You can say what you would do differently

→ That is a better contribution than a fishing expedition that found a p-value. And in a fourteen-week course, it is a much more achievable target.

title: W14. Designing Your Own Project
text:
1) Ten minutes each, in pairs

① State your question in one sentence. Your partner repeats it back. Did they get it right?
② Which quadrant is it in (§2)? Be honest
③ Sketch Figure 2 — the answer figure — on paper. What are the axes?
④ What is your n, and what is the unit of replication?
⑤ Name one confounder that could produce your expected result on its own
⑥ Heading 10 — what would make you stop?







WarningThe three failure modes you will hear most often today






❌ Too broad. “I want to look at the immune microenvironment.” → apply §1 until a comparison appears
❌ n is wrong. “I have 40,000 cells.” → from how many patients? (🔗 W5 §5)
❌ Data does not exist yet. “I’ll collect fresh samples.” → how many will you have in six months? Usually the honest number is under ten

Presentation: 15 minutes + 5 minutes questions.
Background            2 min   the clinical problem
Question              1 min   one sentence, and why it is answerable
Data & methods        3 min   what you had, what you did, what you excluded
Results             5–7 min   your four figures, one message each
Interpretation        2 min   which rung, and what would move it up
